content:
I've been thiking about (and trying to) implementing lean into safety first systems (SIL4), as a matter of fact I'm already into the project and seems to be going surprisingly well on paper, but I've been trying to find any other such projects, and (maybe unsurprisingly) I found none at all.

Developing the entire system directly in Lean 4 and have proofs in the same language seems like a no brainer today, there is no need for multiple translation pipelines, or limitations of such tools, which in the end often end up just being Z3 under the hood.

Has anyone already tried this? What issues can i expect from Lean's compiler memory allocation and runtime surprises? Could it potentially reach (or rival) things like Ada/SPARK? I have found generic papers about implementing formal methods and casually mentioning lean but nothing really substantial.
Hm, I don't know anybody using Lean 4 in SIL4 projects (maybe somebody is out there). That means a lot of investment ($$$) to enable Lean 4 to enter this realm... IOW, you need industrial backing.

Yea the idea was if we assume industrial backing has already started, forgetting about some very important certifications for the time being (which may or may not come years from now), what would be the pitfalls? I've seen some repos for running lean on microcontrollers so having some way of embedding lean's C output into a a high safety microkernel os seems fairly viable, at least as a PoC. Otherwise I suppose using lean jsut as verification and having the code itself in Rust for embedding and using aenas, which tbh I still haven't tried

Marco Simone said:

Has anyone already tried this?

I've been working on something related based on a subset of Lean and compilers that target WASM (with a formal model). https://github.com/jsmorph/leanexe

The goal is to have verified executable artifacts. The statements can prove bounds on heap, traps, etc. There is some bitwise floating point support, too.
